Institute for Digital Inclusion Acceleration (IDIA)

Digital Navigator at the Hive, closing the digital divide one visitor at a time

Timeline: January 2025 - Present
Digital Inclusion Technical Instruction 3D Printing Curriculum Development Community Service

The Mission

IDIA is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit with a clear mandate: everyone deserves the tools to participate in today's digital world, no matter where they live or what their background is. Most jobs now require digital skills, yet one in three workers lacks them, and barriers like device cost, affordable internet, and online safety fall hardest on underserved communities. From the Hive, IDIA's community learning space, we address that gap directly by teaching skills, distributing devices, and meeting people exactly where they are.

What I Do

As a Digital Navigator, I instruct over 300 visitors every week in hardware and software fundamentals. Some are older adults learning to video call their families. Some are students building their first 3D model in TinkerCAD. Some are job seekers formatting a resume on a device they have never touched. I develop and deliver structured curriculum for nine distinct platforms, including Swift, TinkerCAD, and SpheroEDU, and I operate and maintain the center's Flashforge 3D printers, troubleshooting hardware failures and tuning print parameters in Orca Slicer to keep output consistent.

Why This Work Matters to Me

This is the part that does not fit on a resume. I joined IDIA in January 2025, and it remains the most fulfilling work I have ever done. Watching someone's face change when they finally understand a device, or when a printed part comes off the bed clean, genuinely brings me joy. I love this job because it is proof that technology only matters when people can actually use it. That belief shapes the kind of engineer I intend to become: one who builds things people can reach, understand, and rely on.

The Engineering Connection

The Hive is also where I practice engineering in public. Explaining a technical concept to someone with zero technical background is the same discipline as writing clear engineering documentation. Keeping the 3D printers running taught me preventive maintenance, root cause troubleshooting, and the patience to iterate on settings until results are repeatable. Those habits transfer directly to mechanical design, fabrication, and plant operations.

By the Numbers

Nearly two years of continuous service, January 2025 to Present 300+ visitors instructed every week across all age groups 3D printers maintained and operated Nine software platforms with structured, standardized curriculum Thousands of hands-on technology interactions facilitated
